newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden cuts '97 state borrowing need by 10 bln Skr.
newsitem.headline: Sweden cuts '97 state borrowing need by 10 bln Skr.

text.p: Sweden's National Debt Office on Monday lowered its 1997 central government borrowing requirement forecast to 10-20 billion crowns from 20 to 30 billion crowns.
It also forecast the state's borrowing need for June at 5.8 billion crowns and for May it expected a financing surplus of two billion crowns.
The National Debt Office said in a statement the lowering of the borrowing requirement was because of increased tax revenue and lower-than-expected payments by state bodies.
"The reduction in the borrowing requirement is primarily due to revised forecasts for company taxes and supplementary tax payments," the office said in a statement.
"In addition, lower payments by a number of state authorities are expected," it said.
The office said it had also taken into account the government's proposal for a supplementary budget for 1997 which was presented in the spring budget bill.
It said the borrowing requirement for April was 2.1 billion crowns, an increase of 1.3 billion crowns from an earlier forecast.
"The deviation in the result from the forecast is partly explained by higher payments of funds to local authorities than expected," the office said.
The financing surplus of two billion crowns expected for May compares to a previous forecast for a borrowing requirement of 4.2 billion crowns, the office said.
"The improvement by 6.2 billion crowns is primarily explained by unexpectedly large supplementary tax payments in the beginning of the month," it said.

The June figure, a forecast for a borrowing requirement of 5.8 billion crowns, is an increase of one billion crowns from June 1996, explained in part by the fact that several state-owned companies paid dividends to the state in June 1996.
This year dividend payments will be made at different dates.

The borrowing requirement for the 12-month period ending at the end of April totals 12.2 billion crowns. The corresponding figures for May and June are 8.5 billion crowns and 9.5 billion crowns, respectively.
